# 12-Week Strength Programme
### Client Profile: 28F | Recreational Lifter | No Injuries | Full Gym Access

---

## Programme Overview

This programme runs across **three four-week phases**, each with a distinct training stimulus. The structure follows a classic **accumulation → intensification → realisation** model, progressively building volume, then intensity, then peaking for a final performance test. Training frequency is **four days per week**, using an upper/lower split that allows adequate recovery while maximising weekly exposure to each movement pattern.

**Core Lifts Tracked Throughout:**
- Back Squat
- Romanian Deadlift
- Bench Press
- Barbell Row

---

## PHASE 1 — Weeks 1–4: Accumulation (Building the Base)

**Goal:** Establish movement quality, build work capacity, and introduce progressive overload through moderate weight and higher volume. Loads should feel challenging but controlled — aim for **RPE 6–7** on working sets.

---

### Week 1

**Day 1 — Lower Body (Squat Focus)**

Begin each session with 8–10 minutes of general warm-up: rowing machine or bike, followed by dynamic mobility targeting the hips, ankles, and thoracic spine.

- Back Squat — 4 sets × 8 reps @ 65% 1RM
- Romanian Deadlift — 3 sets × 10 reps
- Leg Press — 3 sets × 12 reps
- Walking Lunges — 3 sets × 10 reps each leg
- Leg Curl (machine) — 3 sets × 12 reps
- Plank — 3 × 30 seconds

**Day 2 — Upper Body (Push Focus)**

- Bench Press — 4 sets × 8 reps @ 65% 1RM
- Seated Dumbbell Shoulder Press — 3 sets × 10 reps
- Incline Dumbbell Press — 3 sets × 12 reps
- Lateral Raise — 3 sets × 15 reps
- Tricep Pushdown (cable) — 3 sets × 12 reps
- Dead Bug — 3 × 8 reps each side

**Day 3 — Lower Body (Hinge Focus)**

- Conventional Deadlift — 4 sets × 6 reps @ 65% 1RM
- Goblet Squat — 3 sets × 12 reps
- Hip Thrust (barbell) — 4 sets × 10 reps
- Step-Ups — 3 sets × 10 reps each leg
- Seated Leg Curl — 3 sets × 12 reps
- Side Plank — 3 × 25 seconds each side

**Day 4 — Upper Body (Pull Focus)**

- Barbell Row — 4 sets × 8 reps @ 65% 1RM
- Lat Pulldown — 3 sets × 10 reps
- Seated Cable Row — 3 sets × 12 reps
- Face Pull — 3 sets × 15 reps
- Dumbbell Bicep Curl — 3 sets × 12 reps
- Pallof Press — 3 × 10 reps each side

---

### Weeks 2–4 — Progressive Overload Within Phase 1

Each week, apply the following adjustments to the core lifts and accessory work:

**Week 2:** Increase load by approximately 2.5–5 kg on barbell movements where form was solid. Add one rep to accessory sets where applicable (e.g., 3 × 13 instead of 3 × 12). RPE target remains 6–7.

**Week 3:** Increase load again by 2.5–5 kg on core lifts. Accessory volume holds steady but load increases slightly. Introduce a **tempo prescription** on squat and Romanian deadlift — use a 3-second eccentric (lowering phase) to increase time under tension. RPE creeps to 7–8.

**Week 4 — Deload:** Reduce all working loads by 40–50%. Cut volume to 2–3 sets per exercise. Keep movement patterns identical. This week is not optional — it is where adaptation is consolidated. The client should leave each session feeling refreshed, not fatigued.

---

## PHASE 2 — Weeks 5–8: Intensification (Building Strength)

**Goal:** Shift from volume-led adaptation to intensity-led adaptation. Reps drop, loads climb, and the nervous system is trained to recruit more motor units under heavier demands. RPE target rises to **7–8** on working sets, touching **8–9** on top sets.

The four-day upper/lower structure remains, but sessions are reorganised slightly to prioritise heavier compound work earlier and reduce accessory volume to accommodate the increased loading demands.

---

### Week 5

**Day 1 — Lower Body (Squat Focus)**

- Back Squat — 5 sets × 5 reps @ 75% 1RM
- Romanian Deadlift — 4 sets × 8 reps (heavier than Phase 1)
- Bulgarian Split Squat — 3 sets × 8 reps each leg
- Leg Curl (machine) — 3 sets × 10 reps
- Cable Pull-Through — 3 sets × 12 reps
- Ab Wheel Rollout — 3 × 8 reps

**Day 2 — Upper Body (Push Focus)**

- Bench Press — 5 sets × 5 reps @ 75% 1RM
- Overhead Press (barbell) — 4 sets × 6 reps
- Dumbbell Incline Press — 3 sets × 8 reps
- Cable Lateral Raise — 3 sets × 12 reps
- Skull Crushers — 3 sets × 10 reps
- Hollow Body Hold — 3 × 20 seconds

**Day 3 — Lower Body (Hinge Focus)**

- Conventional Deadlift — 5 sets × 4 reps @ 77.5% 1RM
- Front Squat — 3 sets × 6 reps (technique and quad development)
- Hip Thrust — 4 sets × 8 reps (heavier than Phase 1)
- Nordic Hamstring Curl — 3 sets × 5 reps (eccentric focus)
- Reverse Hyper or Back Extension — 3 sets × 12 reps
- Side Plank with Hip Abduction — 3 × 8 reps each side

**Day 4 — Upper Body (Pull Focus)**

- Barbell Row — 5 sets × 5 reps @ 75% 1RM
- Weighted Pull-Up or Assisted Pull-Up — 4 sets × 5–6 reps
- Single-Arm Dumbbell Row — 3 sets × 8 reps each side
- Face Pull — 3 sets × 12 reps
- Hammer Curl — 3 sets × 10 reps
- Pallof Press — 3 × 8 reps each side

---

### Weeks 6–8 — Progressive Overload Within Phase 2

**Week 6:** Add 2.5–5 kg to all barbell core lifts. Accessory loads increase where the previous week felt below RPE 7. Maintain rep targets precisely — do not sacrifice reps for load.

**Week 7:** Introduce a **top set / back-off set structure** on the four core lifts. Perform one heavy top set at RPE 8–9 (approximately 80–82.5% 1RM), then drop 10% of the load and complete two back-off sets at the prescribed rep range. This exposes the nervous system to near-maximal loads while preserving volume.

**Week 8 — Deload:** Same protocol as Week 4. Loads drop 40–50%, volume reduces to 2–3 sets. Use this week to address any technique issues observed during the heavier weeks. Mobility and soft tissue work should be prioritised.

---

## PHASE 3 — Weeks 9–12: Realisation (Peaking and Testing)

**Goal:** Convert the strength built across Phases 1 and 2 into demonstrated maximal performance. Volume drops significantly, intensity climbs to near-maximal, and the programme culminates in a **testing week** where the client attempts new one-rep maxes on the four core lifts.

---

### Week 9

**Day 1 — Lower Body (Squat Focus)**

- Back Squat — 4 sets × 3 reps @ 82.5% 1RM
- Romanian Deadlift — 3 sets × 6 reps (heavy)
- Bulgarian Split Squat — 3 sets × 6 reps each leg
- Leg Curl — 2 sets × 10 reps
- Plank Variations — 2 × 30–40 seconds

**Day 2 — Upper Body (Push Focus)**

- Bench Press — 4 sets × 3 reps @ 82.5% 1RM
- Overhead Press — 3 sets × 5 reps
- Dumbbell Incline Press — 2 sets × 8 reps
- Lateral Raise — 2 sets × 12 reps
- Tricep Pushdown — 2 sets × 10 reps

**Day 3 — Lower Body (Hinge Focus)**

- Conventional Deadlift — 4 sets × 3 reps @ 82.5% 1RM
- Hip Thrust — 3 sets × 6 reps (heavy)
- Front Squat — 2 sets × 5 reps
- Nordic Hamstring Curl — 2 sets × 4 reps
- Back Extension — 2 sets × 10 reps

**Day 4 — Upper Body (Pull Focus)**

- Barbell Row — 4 sets × 3 reps @ 82.5% 1RM
- Weighted Pull-Up — 3 sets × 4–5 reps
- Single-Arm Row — 2 sets × 8 reps each side
- Face Pull — 2 sets × 12 reps
- Bicep Curl — 2 sets × 10 reps

---

### Weeks 10–11 — Final Intensification

**Week 10:** Move to **3 sets × 2 reps** on core lifts at approximately **87.5% 1RM**. Accessory work reduces to one or two exercises per session, kept at moderate weight. The client should feel powerful and sharp, not ground down.

**Week 11:** Perform **2 sets × 1 rep** on core lifts at **90–92.5% 1RM**. These are heavy singles, not true maxes — they prime the nervous system for Week 12 without causing excessive fatigue. Accessory work is minimal: one exercise per movement pattern, two sets only. Sleep and nutrition become especially important this week.

---

### Week 12 — Testing Week

This is the culmination of twelve weeks of work. The client tests a **one-rep max** on each of the four core lifts across four sessions. Each session follows the same warm-up protocol: begin with the bar, add load in progressively larger jumps (50%, 65%, 75%, 85%, 92.5%), then attempt the true max. Allow **3–5 minutes rest** between heavy attempts. Limit max attempts to three per lift to avoid fatigue-driven failure.

- **Day 1:** Back Squat 1RM
- **Day 2:** Bench Press 1RM
- **Day 3:** Conventional Deadlift 1RM
- **Day 4:** Barbell Row 1RM

Record all results. These numbers become the new baseline percentages for any subsequent programme.

---

## Recovery Guidelines

**Between Sessions:** Aim for a minimum of one full rest day between training days. A recommended weekly schedule is Monday, Tuesday, Thursday, Friday — leaving Wednesday and the weekend for recovery.

**Sleep:** Target 7–9 hours per night. This is non-negotiable for strength adaptation. Poor sleep will blunt progress more than any programming variable.

**Soft Tissue Work:** Encourage 10 minutes of foam rolling and stretching post-session, focusing on the hips, thoracic spine, and lats. This is especially important during Phases 2 and 3 when loading is heaviest.

**Deload Weeks:** Weeks 4 and 8 are structured deloads. The client should not skip these or replace them with extra training. Adaptation happens during recovery, not during the session itself.

---

## General Nutrition Notes

Without a specific nutrition brief, the following principles apply as a foundation:

**Protein:** Prioritise adequate protein intake to support muscle repair and growth — a practical target is **1.6–2.0 g per kg of bodyweight per day**, distributed across meals.

**Carbohydrates:** As training intensity increases across phases, carbohydrate intake around training sessions becomes increasingly important. Encourage a carbohydrate-containing meal 1–2 hours before training and within 1–2 hours after.

**Hydration:** Aim for a minimum of 2–2.5 litres of water daily, more on training days.

**Caloric Context:** If the client's goal is purely strength, a slight caloric surplus of 200–300 kcal above maintenance will support performance and recovery. If body composition is also a consideration, maintenance calories with high protein will allow strength gains while managing body composition.

---

## Coaching Notes

- **Technique always precedes load.** If form breaks down, reduce weight rather than grinding through poor reps. This is especially critical on the squat and deadlift.
- **Log every session.** The client should record weights, reps, and a subjective RPE score. This data is invaluable for making informed load adjustments week to week.
- **Autoregulate when needed.** If the client arrives fatigued, stressed, or under-slept, reduce the day's load by 5–10% and treat it as a technique session. One suboptimal session will not derail the programme; pushing through fatigue recklessly might.
- **Celebrate the deloads.** Many recreational lifters resist backing off. Frame deload weeks as part of the programme, not a break from it.

# Conditioning Sessions — Weekly Addition
### Integrated into the 12-Week Strength Programme

---

## Programming Logic

The two conditioning sessions sit on **Wednesday and Saturday** — the existing rest days — keeping them fully separated from strength work. This protects the quality of both stimuli. Strength sessions remain untouched. The conditioning work is designed to **complement, not compete with**, the lifting by developing aerobic capacity, work capacity, and general fitness without generating excessive fatigue that bleeds into the next strength session.

A key principle here is **interference effect management**. Heavy lower body strength work and high-intensity lower body conditioning done too close together will compromise both. For this reason, Wednesday's session (sitting between two lower body strength days on Tuesday and Thursday) is kept at **low-to-moderate intensity**, while Saturday's session (furthest from any strength work) allows for **higher intensity** effort.

---

## Session Structure by Phase

The conditioning sessions evolve across the three phases in parallel with the strength work — building aerobic base first, then introducing higher intensity, then tapering in the final weeks to protect the peak.

---

## PHASE 1 — Weeks 1–4: Aerobic Base Building

**Goal:** Develop a broad aerobic foundation, improve recovery between strength sessions, and introduce conditioning formats without generating significant muscular fatigue. Intensity is deliberately low to moderate. The client should be able to hold a conversation during Wednesday sessions and feel comfortably challenged but not destroyed on Saturdays.

---

### Wednesday Session — Steady State Cardio (35–40 minutes)

Choose one modality per week, rotating to avoid monotony and develop general fitness across different movement patterns. Good options are the rowing machine, assault bike, ski erg, or incline treadmill walk. Avoid running at high intensity during Phase 1 if the client is not a regular runner — the eccentric loading on untrained legs will create unnecessary soreness ahead of Thursday's lower body session.

- **Intensity:** RPE 4–5. Conversational pace throughout.
- **Structure:** 5-minute warm-up at easy pace, 25–30 minutes at steady state, 5-minute cool-down.
- **Modality rotation example:** Week 1 row, Week 2 bike, Week 3 ski erg, Week 4 incline walk.

During the deload in Week 4, reduce this session to 20 minutes at an even easier pace.

---

### Saturday Session — Circuit Training (30–35 minutes)

A full-body circuit using bodyweight and light implements. The goal is elevated heart rate and movement variety, not muscular failure. Keep rest periods short but not punishing — 20–30 seconds between exercises, 90 seconds between rounds.

**Weeks 1–3 Circuit (4 rounds):**

- Kettlebell Swing — 15 reps
- Box Step-Up — 10 reps each leg
- Push-Up — 12 reps
- TRX or Ring Row — 12 reps
- Goblet Squat — 12 reps
- Battle Rope Slam — 20 reps
- Mountain Climber — 20 reps each leg
- Rest — 90 seconds, then repeat

**Total working time:** Approximately 28–32 minutes depending on pace.

**Week 4 Deload Saturday:** Cut to 2 rounds only, reduce reps by 30%, and extend rest to 2 minutes between rounds.

---

## PHASE 2 — Weeks 5–8: Capacity Development

**Goal:** Now that an aerobic base exists, introduce more structured and demanding conditioning formats. Wednesday remains moderate to protect Thursday's heavy lower body work, but Saturday steps up meaningfully in intensity. The client should be working at RPE 7–8 during Saturday's harder intervals.

---

### Wednesday Session — Tempo Intervals (35–40 minutes)

Tempo intervals sit at a comfortably hard pace — harder than steady state but not all-out. Think of it as the pace where conversation becomes difficult but not impossible. This format builds lactate threshold without the deep fatigue of true high-intensity work.

- **Structure:** 5-minute warm-up, then 6 × 4-minute intervals at RPE 6–7, with 90-second easy recovery between each, followed by a 5-minute cool-down.
- **Modality:** Rowing machine or assault bike preferred. These are low-impact and spare the legs more than running.
- **Progression across weeks:** Week 5 uses 6 × 3 minutes to introduce the format. Week 6 moves to 6 × 4 minutes. Week 7 extends to 5 × 5 minutes. Week 8 deload returns to 4 × 3 minutes at RPE 5.

---

### Saturday Session — AMRAP and EMOM Formats (35–40 minutes)

These formats introduce structured intensity and teach the client to manage effort across a defined time window — a useful skill for general fitness and mental toughness.

**Weeks 5 and 6 — AMRAP Format (As Many Rounds As Possible):**

Perform as many rounds as possible in 20 minutes of the following circuit. Record the number of rounds completed each week to track progress.

- Kettlebell Deadlift — 10 reps
- Dumbbell Push Press — 10 reps
- Calorie Row — 10 calories
- Burpee — 8 reps
- Dumbbell Reverse Lunge — 8 reps each leg

Rest as needed but minimise it. The goal is consistent, sustainable effort — not sprinting the first three rounds and collapsing. Follow with 10 minutes of steady-state cool-down on the bike.

**Weeks 7 — EMOM Format (Every Minute On the Minute):**

Set a 24-minute clock. Every minute on the minute, perform the prescribed work, then rest for the remainder of that minute before the next minute begins. Rotate through three stations in sequence.

- Minute A: 12 Kettlebell Swings
- Minute B: 10 Push-Ups + 5 Burpees
- Minute C: 14 Calorie Assault Bike

Repeat the A–B–C sequence 8 times for 24 total minutes. The rest within each minute is the reward for working efficiently — if the client is consistently getting less than 15 seconds of rest, reduce the rep count slightly.

**Week 8 Deload Saturday:** Return to the Phase 1 circuit format, 3 rounds only, at easy effort. This is active recovery, not training.

---

## PHASE 3 — Weeks 9–12: Taper and Maintenance

**Goal:** As strength training intensity peaks, conditioning volume and intensity must be managed carefully. The priority in this phase is arriving at Week 12's testing sessions fresh and powerful. Conditioning sessions shift to **maintenance mode** — enough stimulus to preserve fitness gains without generating fatigue that undermines the 1RM tests.

---

### Wednesday Session — Easy Aerobic Maintenance (25–30 minutes)

- **Weeks 9–10:** 25 minutes of steady-state work at RPE 4–5. Any modality. No intervals. This is a recovery-enhancing session, not a fitness-building one.
- **Week 11:** Reduce to 20 minutes at RPE 4. Keep it genuinely easy. The nervous system is under significant stress from near-maximal lifting — do not add to that burden.
- **Week 12 (Testing Week):** Replace the conditioning session entirely with 15–20 minutes of light movement — a walk, easy bike, or mobility flow. The client needs to be fresh for their 1RM attempts.

---

### Saturday Session — Short, Sharp Conditioning (25–30 minutes)

**Weeks 9–10 — Short Interval Work:**

The format shifts to shorter, more explosive intervals that maintain power output and conditioning without accumulating the deep fatigue of longer circuits.

- 10-minute easy warm-up on the rower or bike
- 8 × 30-second hard efforts at RPE 8, with 90-second full rest between each
- 10-minute easy cool-down

Total session time: approximately 28 minutes. The hard efforts should feel genuinely fast and powerful — this is sprint-quality work, not tempo. The generous rest ratio (1:3 work-to-rest) ensures each interval is high quality.

**Week 11 — Further Taper:**

- 10-minute warm-up
- 5 × 20-second hard efforts at RPE 8, with 2-minute full rest between each
- 10-minute cool-down

Total session time: approximately 25 minutes. Volume is minimal. The purpose is to keep the neuromuscular system primed and the client feeling athletic without adding any meaningful fatigue load.

**Week 12 (Testing Week):** Cancel the Saturday conditioning session entirely. The client should rest, eat well, sleep, and prepare mentally for any remaining 1RM tests.

---

|---|---|
| **Monday** | Strength — Lower Body (Squat Focus) |
| **Tuesday** | Strength — Upper Body (Push Focus) |
| **Wednesday** | Conditioning — Moderate Intensity |
| **Thursday** | Strength — Lower Body (Hinge Focus) |
| **Friday** | Strength — Upper Body (Pull Focus) |
| **Saturday** | Conditioning — Higher Intensity |

---

## Nutrition Adjustment for Conditioning Days

With two additional sessions per week, total energy expenditure increases meaningfully. A few practical adjustments are worth flagging:

**Caloric intake on conditioning days** should be slightly higher than rest days — an additional 150–250 kcal, primarily from carbohydrates, will fuel the sessions and support recovery without overcomplicating the approach.

**Pre-conditioning nutrition** follows the same principle as strength days — a carbohydrate-containing meal or snack 1–2 hours before the session. On Wednesday in particular, where the session sits between two strength days, arriving fuelled matters.

**Hydration** becomes more important with six active days per week. Encourage the client to monitor urine colour as a simple hydration check — pale yellow is the target.

---

## Coaching Notes on Conditioning

- **Protect Thursday.** Wednesday's session should never leave the client so fatigued that Thursday's lower body strength work suffers. If she arrives to Thursday's session with heavy legs, Wednesday's intensity needs to come down.
- **Track conditioning metrics too.** Recording Saturday AMRAP rounds, interval times, or perceived effort gives the client a second set of progress markers beyond the barbell — this is motivating and informative.
- **Modality flexibility.** If the client strongly dislikes a particular modality, swap it. The physiological goal of each session matters more than the specific tool used to achieve it. A hated session done half-heartedly is worse than an enjoyed session done with full effort.
- **Phase 3 is not the time to push conditioning.** Some clients will feel fit and want to maintain Saturday intensity into Weeks 11 and 12. Redirect that energy toward the 1RM tests. The conditioning fitness will not disappear in two weeks of tapering — but accumulated fatigue absolutely will affect the peak.

# Posterior-Chain Revision
### Deadlift-Focused Reprogramming

---

## What Changes and Why

The original programme treated the four core lifts with roughly equal priority. With deadlift strength as the primary goal, the architecture needs to shift. The conventional deadlift moves to the **top of the training hierarchy**, and the entire lower body structure is rebuilt around it. This means more frequent hinge-pattern exposure, greater volume directed at the glutes and hamstrings, and accessory selection that directly feeds deadlift performance — namely the spinal erectors, lats, upper back, and hip extensors.

The squat remains in the programme because it builds the quad strength and positional stability that supports a strong pull off the floor. The upper body days are largely preserved but adjusted where pulling movements can do double duty for the back musculature that matters in the deadlift. The bench press stays as a structural balance tool and because the client is still a recreational lifter with general fitness goals.

Three principles drive every change made below:

**First**, the deadlift is trained with the highest priority in each week — it appears earliest in the week when the client is freshest, and the heaviest lower body session is always built around the hinge, not the squat.

**Second**, posterior-chain accessory work is significantly expanded. Romanian deadlifts, good mornings, glute-ham raises, back extensions, Nordic hamstring curls, and hip thrusts all appear with greater frequency and volume than in the original plan.

**Third**, the upper back receives more direct attention. A strong deadlift requires the lats to be braced hard against the bar, the upper back to stay tight, and the traps to control the load at lockout. Pull-up variations, heavy rows, shrugs, and face pulls are all programmed with this in mind.

---

## Revised Exercise Hierarchy

**Primary — Deadlift Variations (trained twice weekly):**
- Conventional Deadlift — main strength expression
- Romanian Deadlift — hamstring length and loading under stretch
- Deficit Deadlift — introduced in Phase 2 to build strength off the floor
- Pause Deadlift — introduced in Phase 2 to address the sticking point just below the knee

**Primary — Squat (retained, reduced priority):**
- Back Squat — positional strength and quad development
- Front Squat — upper back and positional demands carry over to deadlift setup

**Posterior-Chain Accessories (high priority):**
- Glute-Ham Raise
- Nordic Hamstring Curl
- Back Extension / Reverse Hyper
- Good Morning
- Hip Thrust
- Cable Pull-Through
- Kettlebell Swing

**Upper Back Accessories (high priority):**
- Weighted Pull-Up
- Pendlay Row
- Chest-Supported Row
- Barbell Shrug
- Face Pull
- Band Pull-Apart

---

## Revised Weekly Structure

The split shifts from a symmetrical upper/lower to a **deadlift-led lower/upper/lower/upper** structure where the two lower days are clearly differentiated — one hinge-dominant, one squat-dominant — and the upper days both carry meaningful upper back volume.

| Day | Session |
|---|---|
| **Monday** | Lower — Hinge Focus (Deadlift Primary) |
| **Tuesday** | Upper — Pull Focus (Heavy Row + Upper Back) |
| **Wednesday** | Conditioning |
| **Thursday** | Lower — Squat Focus (Posterior Chain Accessories) |
| **Friday** | Upper — Push + Upper Back Accessory |
| **Saturday** | Conditioning |
| **Sunday** | Full Rest |

Monday is the most important session of the week. The client is freshest, the nervous system is recovered from the weekend, and the deadlift gets the best version of her every single week.

---

## PHASE 1 — Weeks 1–4: Posterior Chain Accumulation

**Goal:** Build volume tolerance in the hinge pattern, develop hamstring and glute hypertrophy that will underpin later strength gains, and establish the upper back work capacity needed for heavy pulling. Loads remain moderate — RPE 6–7 — but volume is deliberately high to drive adaptation in the target musculature.

---

### Week 1

**Monday — Lower Body: Hinge Focus**

Warm-up: 8 minutes on the rowing machine, followed by hip 90/90 stretches, banded clamshells, and cat-cow. The rowing machine is the preferred warm-up tool throughout this programme — it primes the hinge pattern, warms the posterior chain, and reinforces the same back position used in the deadlift.

- Conventional Deadlift — 4 sets × 6 reps @ 65% 1RM. Focus on lat engagement, bracing, and a controlled eccentric. Do not rush the setup between reps — treat each rep as a single.
- Romanian Deadlift — 4 sets × 10 reps. Load moderately. Feel the hamstring stretch at the bottom — this is the point of the exercise. Hinge until the bar passes the knee and a strong pull is felt in the hamstrings, then drive the hips through.
- Hip Thrust (barbell) — 3 sets × 12 reps. Full hip extension at the top, pause for one second, controlled descent.
- Back Extension — 3 sets × 15 reps. Bodyweight or light plate held at chest. Focus on glute and hamstring initiation, not lower back hyperextension.
- Leg Curl (machine) — 3 sets × 12 reps.
- Dead Bug — 3 × 8 reps each side. Core stability is a deadlift prerequisite — it earns its place in every lower body session.

**Tuesday — Upper Body: Pull Focus**

Warm-up: Band pull-aparts, 2 × 15. Scapular retractions on the bar. This primes the upper back before any loaded pulling.

- Barbell Row (Pendlay style) — 4 sets × 8 reps @ 65% 1RM. Pendlay rows — where the bar returns to the floor between each rep — are preferred over traditional bent-over rows here because they reinforce the same flat-back hinge position used in the deadlift and allow heavier loading.
- Weighted Pull-Up or Lat Pulldown — 4 sets × 6–8 reps. If the client cannot yet perform weighted pull-ups, use lat pulldown and build toward bodyweight pull-ups across the programme.
- Chest-Supported Dumbbell Row — 3 sets × 10 reps each side. The chest support removes lower back fatigue from the equation and allows the upper back to be trained in isolation.
- Barbell Shrug — 3 sets × 12 reps. Trap strength is directly relevant to deadlift lockout. Hold the top position for one second.
- Face Pull — 4 sets × 15 reps. High rep, moderate load. Rear delt and external rotator health.
- Band Pull-Apart — 3 × 20 reps. Superset with face pulls to maximise upper back pump and reinforce scapular retraction.

**Thursday — Lower Body: Squat Focus with Posterior Chain Accessories**

Warm-up: Same as Monday — rowing machine, hip mobility, banded activation.

- Back Squat — 4 sets × 8 reps @ 65% 1RM. The squat serves the deadlift here. Cue the client to think about the same lat engagement and bracing used in the pull.
- Good Morning — 3 sets × 10 reps. Light load, strict form. This exercise directly trains the spinal erectors and hamstrings in the same position as the deadlift — it is one of the most underused deadlift accessories available.
- Walking Lunge — 3 sets × 10 reps each leg.
- Glute-Ham Raise — 3 sets × 6–8 reps. If the client is new to this movement, begin with a partial range of motion and build over the weeks. This is one of the most effective hamstring exercises in existence and will pay dividends on the deadlift.
- Cable Pull-Through — 3 sets × 15 reps. Reinforces the hip hinge pattern with a lighter load — excellent for building the feel of driving the hips through at lockout.
- Pallof Press — 3 × 10 reps each side.

**Friday — Upper Body: Push with Upper Back Accessory**

Warm-up: Band pull-aparts, shoulder circles, light face pulls.

- Bench Press — 4 sets × 8 reps @ 65% 1RM.
- Overhead Press (barbell) — 3 sets × 10 reps.
- Incline Dumbbell Press — 3 sets × 12 reps.
- Chest-Supported Row — 3 sets × 10 reps. Upper back work appears on the push day too — the deadlift demands it.
- Face Pull — 3 sets × 15 reps.
- Lateral Raise — 3 sets × 15 reps.
- Tricep Pushdown — 3 sets × 12 reps.

---

### Weeks 2–4 Progression Within Phase 1

**Week 2:** Add 2.5–5 kg to the conventional deadlift and Pendlay row. Increase Romanian deadlift load slightly. Add one rep to all accessory sets where the previous week felt below RPE 7. Introduce a **3-second eccentric** on the Romanian deadlift — this dramatically increases hamstring time under tension and is one of the most effective hypertrophy tools available for the posterior chain.

**Week 3:** Add load again to the deadlift and row. Introduce a **pause at the floor** on the conventional deadlift — after lowering the bar, pause for two seconds, reset the brace and lat engagement, then pull again. This eliminates any bounce reflex and builds starting strength, which is where most recreational lifters are weakest. Glute-ham raise reps increase to 8–10 as the movement becomes more familiar.

**Week 4 — Deload:** Reduce all loads by 40–50%, cut to 2–3 sets per exercise. Keep the movement patterns identical. On the deadlift, use this week to film the client's pull from the side and review setup, bar path, and lockout mechanics. Technique refinement during a deload is time extremely well spent.

---

## PHASE 2 — Weeks 5–8: Deadlift Intensification

**Goal:** Load climbs, rep ranges drop, and two deadlift variations are introduced to address specific weaknesses in the pull. The deficit deadlift builds strength off the floor — the most common sticking point. The pause deadlift reinforces position just below the knee — the second most common sticking point. Both variations are trained at slightly lower intensities than the conventional pull but contribute meaningfully to overall deadlift strength. RPE target on working sets is **7–8**, touching **8–9** on top sets by Week 7.

---

### Week 5

**Monday — Lower Body: Hinge Focus**

Warm-up: Rowing machine, hip 90/90, banded clamshells, one set of back extensions with bodyweight.

- Conventional Deadlift — 5 sets × 4 reps @ 77.5% 1RM. Rest 3 full minutes between sets. The deadlift is the most taxing movement in the programme — it deserves the most rest.
- Deficit Deadlift — 3 sets × 4 reps @ 65% 1RM. Stand on a 2.5 cm plate or bumper plate. The increased range of motion demands more from the hamstrings and glutes at the initiation of the pull. Keep loads conservative — this is a technique and strength-building tool, not a max effort exercise.
- Romanian Deadlift — 4 sets × 8 reps (heavier than Phase 1, 3-second eccentric maintained).
- Hip Thrust — 4 sets × 8 reps (heavier than Phase 1).
- Nordic Hamstring Curl — 3 sets × 5 reps. Eccentric focus — lower as slowly as possible, use hands to return to the top. This is brutally effective for hamstring strength and injury resilience.
- Ab Wheel Rollout — 3 × 8 reps. Anti-extension core strength is directly relevant to maintaining a neutral spine under a heavy deadlift.

**Tuesday — Upper Body: Pull Focus**

- Pendlay Row — 5 sets × 5 reps @ 75% 1RM.
- Weighted Pull-Up — 4 sets × 5 reps. Add load progressively each week.
- Single-Arm Dumbbell Row — 3 sets × 8 reps each side. Heavy. Brace the core as if setting up for a deadlift.
- Barbell Shrug — 4 sets × 8 reps. Heavier than Phase 1. Hold the top for two seconds.
- Face Pull — 3 sets × 12 reps.
- Band Pull-Apart — 3 × 20 reps.

**Thursday — Lower Body: Squat Focus**

- Back Squat — 4 sets × 5 reps @ 75% 1RM.
- Good Morning — 4 sets × 8 reps (heavier than Phase 1). This exercise should feel genuinely challenging by Week 6.
- Bulgarian Split Squat — 3 sets × 8 reps each leg.
- Glute-Ham Raise — 4 sets × 8 reps. Full range of motion now that the movement is established.
- Back Extension — 3 sets × 12 reps with a plate held at chest.
- Reverse Hyper (if available) — 3 sets × 15 reps. Excellent for spinal erector development and lower back recovery simultaneously.
- Pallof Press — 3 × 8 reps each side.

**Friday — Upper Body: Push with Upper Back**

- Bench Press — 4 sets × 5 reps @ 75% 1RM.
- Overhead Press — 3 sets × 6 reps.
- Incline Dumbbell Press — 3 sets × 8 reps.
- Chest-Supported Row — 3 sets × 8 reps (heavier than Phase 1).
- Face Pull — 3 sets × 12 reps.
- Lateral Raise — 3 sets × 12 reps.
- Skull Crusher — 3 sets × 10 reps.

---

### Weeks 6–8 Progression Within Phase 2

**Week 6:** Add 2.5–5 kg to the conventional deadlift and Pendlay row. Increase deficit deadlift load slightly. The Romanian deadlift load increases — by this point the client should be handling meaningfully more than her Phase 1 weights. Nordic hamstring curl reps increase to 6.

**Week 7:** Introduce the **top set / back-off structure** on the conventional deadlift. Perform one top set at RPE 8–9 — approximately 82.5–85% 1RM — then drop 10% and complete two back-off sets of 3 reps. This is the most important week of Phase 2. Also introduce the **pause deadlift** this week, replacing the deficit deadlift: perform 3 sets × 3 reps with a 2-second pause just below the knee. Load at approximately 70% 1RM. The pause forces the client to maintain position at the most mechanically demanding point of the lift.

With significantly more hamstring and glute volume than the original programme, **muscle protein synthesis demands increase**. ## Coaching Notes — Deadlift Specific

- **The setup is half the lift.** Spend time in early sessions drilling the pre-pull routine: foot position, hip hinge to the bar, lat engagement cue ("protect your armpits" or "bend the bar around your legs"), deep breath and brace, then pull. A consistent setup routine eliminates variables and builds confidence under heavy loads.
- **Film every heavy set.** The deadlift is uniquely difficult to self-assess. A side-on video of every working set above 80% allows both trainer and client to monitor bar path, back position, and hip rise. Catching a technical breakdown at 85% prevents a failed attempt at 95%.
- **Grip will become a limiting factor.** As loads climb into Phase 2 and 3, grip strength may limit what the posterior chain can actually lift. Introduce a **mixed grip** (one hand over, one hand under) for top sets if double overhand grip fails. Alternatively, use chalk and train double overhand as long as possible to build grip strength as a genuine asset.
- **Lower back fatigue is a signal, not a badge of honour.** Some erector fatigue after heavy deadlift sessions is normal. Persistent soreness, tightness that doesn't resolve by the next session, or any sharp pain is a signal to reduce load and assess technique. The reverse hyper and back extension, programmed at moderate loads, serve a recovery function as much as a strength function — they pump blood into the erectors without loading them heavily.
- **Celebrate posterior chain progress beyond the 1RM.** Track Romanian deadlift loads, glute-ham raise reps, and hip thrust weights alongside the conventional deadlift. These numbers tell the story of the posterior chain development that is making the main lift stronger.

# Revised Programme — Hamstring Strain Management
### Grade I Strain, Right Hamstring | Physio Restriction: 4–6 Weeks Light Lower Body, No Posterior-Chain Loading

---

## Immediate Assessment and Replanning Logic

First, the important framing. A Grade I hamstring strain is a partial tear of a small number of muscle fibres — painful and frustrating, but genuinely manageable with the right approach. The physio's restriction of 4–6 weeks with no posterior-chain loading is the non-negotiable boundary around which everything below is built. Violating that boundary risks converting a Grade I into a Grade II or III, which would end the programme entirely and potentially sideline the client for months. The restriction is respected absolutely.

She was injured on Friday of Week 2. She has completed two full weeks of training. The replanning begins from Week 3.

The revised plan has four components working simultaneously. **First**, the lower body is managed conservatively — quad-dominant movements only, within pain-free range, at low loads. **Second**, the upper body becomes the primary training stimulus for the next four to six weeks, with volume and intensity increased meaningfully to maintain progress and give the client something to work toward. **Third**, the conditioning sessions are modified to remove any hamstring demand. **Fourth**, a structured **return-to-loading protocol** is built into Weeks 7–12 that reintroduces posterior-chain work progressively, respects the healing timeline, and rebuilds toward the original deadlift goal.

The original 12-week endpoint is preserved. The programme simply takes a different route to get there.

One critical note before proceeding: **this plan is built around the physio's current guidance**. If the physio's assessment changes at any point — either clearing the client sooner or extending the restriction — the programme must be updated accordingly. The trainer should maintain communication with the physio throughout the restricted phase and at the 4-week and 6-week marks specifically.

---

## Revised Programme Architecture

| Phase | Weeks | Focus |
|---|---|---|
| **Phase A** | Weeks 3–4 | Injury Management — Upper Body Priority, Quad-Only Lower |
| **Phase B** | Weeks 5–6 | Upper Body Intensification — Continued Conservative Lower |
| **Phase C** | Weeks 7–8 | Graduated Return — Light Posterior Chain Reintroduction (physio clearance required) |
| **Phase D** | Weeks 9–10 | Posterior Chain Rebuilding — Moderate Loading |
| **Phase E** | Weeks 11–12 | Strength Realisation — Modified Peak and Testing |

## PHASE A — Weeks 3–4: Injury Management

**Goal:** Protect the healing hamstring completely. Maintain lower body movement patterns through quad-dominant work that places zero load on the posterior chain. Increase upper body volume to preserve overall training stimulus and give the client a productive focus during a frustrating period. Keep conditioning entirely upper-body and cardiovascular — no hip hinge, no knee flexion under load, nothing that stretches or contracts the hamstring against resistance.

A note on pain: during this phase, **zero pain is the standard**. Not low pain, not manageable pain — zero. If any exercise produces discomfort in the right hamstring, it is removed immediately.

---

### Week 3

**Monday — Lower Body: Quad Focus Only**

Warm-up: 8 minutes on the stationary bike at easy pace. The bike is the preferred warm-up tool during the restricted phase — it keeps the knee moving through a comfortable range without loading the hamstring. Avoid the rowing machine entirely until clearance is given, as the rowing stroke involves significant hamstring engagement.

- Leg Press (bilateral) — 3 sets × 12 reps. Moderate load. Feet positioned mid-platform to emphasise quads. Ensure the range of motion does not pull into hamstring stretch — stop the descent before any posterior-chain tension is felt.
- Leg Extension — 3 sets × 15 reps. Pure quad isolation. This is one of the few lower body machines that loads the quads with essentially no hamstring involvement.
- Wall Sit — 3 × 30 seconds. Isometric quad loading, zero hamstring demand.
- Step-Up (low box, bodyweight only) — 3 sets × 10 reps each leg. Keep the box height low enough that the hip does not hinge significantly. Focus on the quad driving the movement.
- Seated Calf Raise — 3 sets × 15 reps. Maintains lower leg work without any hamstring involvement.

No deadlifts, no Romanian deadlifts, no hip thrusts, no back extensions, no good mornings, no lunges (which involve a hamstring stretch at the bottom), no leg curls. None of these return until physio clearance.

## PHASE C — Weeks 7–8: Graduated Posterior Chain Return
### Physio Clearance Required Before Beginning This Phase

**Goal:** Reintroduce posterior-chain loading with extreme conservatism. The principle here is **start lighter than feels necessary and progress slower than feels necessary**. A Grade I strain that is rushed back into loading can easily become a Grade II. The client will be eager to return to deadlifts — manage that eagerness carefully. Nothing heavier than bodyweight or very light loads in Week 7. Pain remains the absolute stop signal.

The return-to-loading sequence follows a logical progression: **isometric first, then bodyweight concentric, then light loaded, then moderate loaded**. By the end of Phase C the client should be performing light Romanian deadlifts and hip thrusts with a load that feels almost embarrassingly easy. That is correct. The load will climb quickly in Phase D once the tissue has demonstrated it can tolerate the movement pattern.

A practical starting point for the conventional deadlift in Week 9 is approximately **50–55% of the pre-injury working load**. If she was pulling 4 × 6 at 65% of her 1RM before the injury, begin at roughly 50% of her 1RM with reduced volume. The load will climb quickly if the tissue responds well.

# Upper Body Priority Plan
### Keeping Progress Moving During Hamstring Rehabilitation

---

## The Conversation First

Before the programming, acknowledge the frustration directly with your client. A hamstring strain four weeks into a programme she was genuinely invested in is demoralising. The instinct is to push through or catastrophise — neither serves her. What actually helps is reframing the situation honestly: her upper body has been the secondary priority in this programme so far. For the next four to six weeks, it becomes the entire focus. The bench press, overhead press, row, and pull-up are about to receive the kind of dedicated attention they rarely get when someone is also squatting and deadlifting heavy three times a week. She will come out of this period with a meaningfully stronger upper body and a healthier hamstring. That is not a consolation prize — it is a legitimate training outcome.

---

## Programming Logic

With lower body work reduced to gentle quad-only maintenance, the upper body can absorb significantly more volume and frequency than it was receiving before. In the original programme she was training each upper body movement pattern twice a week across two sessions. The revised plan moves to **four dedicated upper body sessions per week** — two push-focused, two pull-focused — with total weekly upper body volume roughly doubling. This is well within recoverable range given that lower body fatigue is essentially removed from the equation.

The structure uses a **push/pull split across four days** rather than the previous upper/lower arrangement. This allows each session to be focused and high quality without becoming excessively long. Each session targets one primary movement for strength development, supported by accessory work that builds the muscles feeding that primary lift.

Two clear strength goals are set for the upper body phase, giving the client concrete targets to chase:

**Goal 1 — Bench Press:** Add 5–10 kg to her working 5-rep load by the time full training resumes.

**Goal 2 — Weighted Pull-Up:** Increase the load on her working pull-up sets by 5–7.5 kg, or if she is currently on lat pulldown, achieve her first strict bodyweight pull-up.

These goals are specific, measurable, and achievable within the timeframe. Write them down with her. Progress toward them becomes the narrative of the next four to six weeks.

---

## Weekly Structure

| Day | Session |
|---|---|
| **Monday** | Push A — Bench Press Primary |
| **Tuesday** | Pull A — Row Primary |
| **Wednesday** | Conditioning (upper body and cardio only) |
| **Thursday** | Push B — Overhead Press Primary |
| **Friday** | Pull B — Pull-Up and Upper Back Primary |
| **Saturday** | Conditioning (upper body and cardio only) |
| **Sunday** | Full Rest |

Lower body on Monday and Thursday is retained as a brief quad-only block — 15–20 minutes maximum — bolted onto the end of those sessions. It does not interfere with the upper body work and keeps the legs ticking over without loading the hamstring.

---

## Exercise Selection and Rationale

Before laying out the weeks, it is worth being explicit about why each movement is chosen and what it contributes. When a client is frustrated and feeling limited, understanding the purpose of what they are doing increases buy-in considerably.

**Bench Press** is the primary horizontal push and the most straightforward strength marker to track. It receives the most dedicated programming attention of the push movements.

**Overhead Press** develops the anterior deltoid, upper traps, and triceps in a way the bench press does not. A stronger overhead press feeds back into bench press performance and builds the shoulder stability that will matter when deadlifting resumes.

**Dips** are introduced as a secondary pressing movement. They allow a greater range of motion than the bench press, load the lower pec and tricep heavily, and provide a useful variation that reduces the repetitive stress of pressing from a fixed position every session.

**Pendlay Row** remains the primary horizontal pull. It is kept heavy and treated with the same seriousness as the bench press. Upper back strength built here will directly transfer back to the deadlift.

**Weighted Pull-Up** is the primary vertical pull and one of the most effective upper body strength exercises available. Progressing this movement over the next four to six weeks will produce visible and functional results.

**Chest-Supported Row** removes lower back fatigue entirely and allows the upper back to be trained in isolation. With no deadlifting happening, this becomes an important tool for maintaining upper back development.

**Face Pull and Band Pull-Apart** appear in every session in some form. With pressing frequency doubled, the posterior shoulder and rotator cuff need consistent attention to stay healthy. These are not optional accessories — they are injury prevention work.

## The Programme — Week by Week

### Week 3 — Establishing the New Structure

The priority this week is establishing the four-session rhythm and assessing where the client actually is on each upper body movement. Loads should be based on what she was lifting in Weeks 1 and 2, but treat this as a re-establishment week rather than a maximum effort week. RPE target across all working sets is **6–7**. There will be a temptation to push hard immediately — resist it. The volume increase alone will be a sufficient stimulus this week.

---

**Monday — Push A: Bench Press Primary**

Warm-up: 5 minutes on the stationary bike, then band pull-aparts 2 × 20, shoulder circles, and two light warm-up sets on the bench.

- Bench Press — 5 sets × 5 reps. Use the load from Week 2 or reduce by 5% to account for the new volume context. Rest 2.5–3 minutes between sets.
- Incline Dumbbell Press — 4 sets × 10 reps. Moderate load. The incline angle shifts emphasis to the upper pec and anterior delt — a region that responds well to dedicated volume.
- Cable Fly — 3 sets × 12 reps. Constant tension through the pec. Keep the load light enough to feel a genuine stretch at the bottom of each rep.
- Overhead Press (barbell) — 3 sets × 8 reps. Treated as an accessory to the bench press today — moderate load, focus on technique.
- Lateral Raise — 4 sets × 15 reps. High rep, moderate load. The medial delt is chronically undertrained in most recreational lifters and responds well to volume.
- Tricep Pushdown (cable) — 3 sets × 12 reps.
- Skull Crusher — 3 sets × 10 reps.
- Face Pull — 3 sets × 15 reps. Finish every push session with face pulls. Non-negotiable.

*Lower body add-on (15 minutes):*
- Leg Press — 3 sets × 12 reps
- Leg Extension — 3 sets × 15 reps
- Terminal Knee Extension — 2 sets × 15 reps each leg

---

**Tuesday — Pull A: Row Primary**

Warm-up: Band pull-aparts 2 × 20, scapular retractions, light face pulls.

- Pendlay Row — 5 sets × 5 reps. Maintain Week 2 load or add 2.5 kg if Week 2 felt below RPE 7.
- Chest-Supported Dumbbell Row — 4 sets × 10 reps each side. Controlled, full range of motion. Squeeze the shoulder blade at the top of each rep.
- Single-Arm Cable Row — 3 sets × 12 reps each side. The cable provides constant tension throughout the range of motion, which the dumbbell row does not. Both have value and both are kept.
- Barbell Shrug — 4 sets × 12 reps. Moderate load, 2-second hold at the top. Trap development feeds directly into deadlift lockout — keep training it even while the deadlift is absent.
- Face Pull — 4 sets × 15 reps.
- Band Pull-Apart — 3 × 20 reps. Superset with face pulls.
- Dumbbell Bicep Curl — 4 sets × 12 reps.
- Hammer Curl — 3 sets × 12 reps.

---

**Thursday — Push B: Overhead Press Primary**

Warm-up: Stationary bike 5 minutes, band pull-aparts 2 × 20, shoulder circles, two light warm-up sets on the overhead press.

- Overhead Press (barbell) — 5 sets × 5 reps. This is now a primary lift with its own dedicated session. Use a load that represents a genuine challenge at 5 reps — RPE 7 on the first set, building to RPE 8 by the fifth set.
- Push Press — 3 sets × 5 reps. A slight leg drive is used to initiate the movement, allowing a heavier load than the strict press. This overloads the lockout position and builds confidence with heavier weight overhead.
- Dips — 4 sets × 8 reps. Bodyweight to start. If bodyweight feels easy, add a dumbbell between the thighs or use a dip belt. If bodyweight is too challenging, use the assisted dip machine.
- Incline Dumbbell Press — 3 sets × 10 reps.
- Cable Lateral Raise — 4 sets × 15 reps. Cable version maintains tension at the bottom of the movement where the dumbbell version goes slack.
- Tricep Overhead Extension (cable or dumbbell) — 3 sets × 12 reps. The long head of the tricep is best trained in a stretched position — overhead extensions achieve this where pushdowns do not.
- Face Pull — 3 sets × 15 reps.
- Band Pull-Apart — 3 × 20 reps.

*Lower body add-on (15 minutes):*
- Hack Squat — 3 sets × 10 reps
- Leg Extension — 3 sets × 12 reps
- Terminal Knee Extension — 2 sets × 15 reps each leg

---

**Friday — Pull B: Pull-Up and Upper Back Primary**

Warm-up: Band pull-aparts 2 × 20, dead hangs 2 × 20 seconds, scapular pull-ups 2 × 8.

- Weighted Pull-Up or Lat Pulldown — 5 sets × 5 reps. If performing weighted pull-ups, add the minimum available load above bodyweight. If on lat pulldown, use a load that makes 5 reps genuinely challenging. This is the primary vertical pull and it is treated with the same seriousness as the bench press and overhead press.
- Pull-Up Cluster Sets — 3 clusters of 10 total reps with 20 seconds rest within each cluster. For example: 4 reps, rest 20 seconds, 3 reps, rest 20 seconds, 3 reps. This technique accumulates pull-up volume beyond what straight sets allow and is one of the most effective tools for building pull-up strength. Use bodyweight only.
- Chest-Supported Row — 4 sets × 10 reps (heavier than Tuesday).
- Straight-Arm Pulldown (cable) — 3 sets × 12 reps. This exercise isolates the lat without involving the bicep, building the lat strength that will be critical for keeping the bar close to the body when deadlifting resumes.
- Barbell Shrug — 3 sets × 10 reps.
- Face Pull — 4 sets × 15 reps.
- Band Pull-Apart — 3 × 20 reps.
- Incline Dumbbell Curl — 3 sets × 10 reps. The incline position stretches the bicep at the bottom, increasing the range of motion and the training stimulus.
- Reverse Curl — 3 sets × 12 reps. Trains the brachialis and brachioradialis — important for elbow health and grip strength, both of which matter for the deadlift.

---

### Week 4 — Load Progression

Week 4 was originally a deload. **That deload is cancelled.** The client has only been at the new upper body volume for one week — a deload now would interrupt adaptation before it has had a chance to take hold. Instead, Week 4 applies the first meaningful load increases.

Add **2.5–5 kg** to the bench press, overhead press, and Pendlay row where Week 3 felt below RPE 8 on the final set. Increase dumbbell loads on accessory movements where appropriate. Add **2.5 kg** to the weighted pull-up if Week 3 felt manageable.

One structural addition this week: introduce **paused reps** on the bench press. Perform the final two sets of the bench press with a 2-second pause at the bottom — bar touching the chest, full pause, then press. This eliminates any bounce reflex, builds starting strength off the chest, and increases time under tension in the pec. It is one of the most effective bench press strength tools available and costs nothing in terms of equipment or session time.

---

### Week 5 — Intensification Begins

Rep ranges on the primary lifts drop and loads climb. The client is now two weeks into the new structure and the movement patterns are established. It is time to push.

**Primary lift prescription for Week 5:**

- Bench Press — 5 sets × 4 reps @ 80% 1RM. The final set should be RPE 8–9.
- Overhead Press — 5 sets × 4 reps @ 80% 1RM.
- Pendlay Row — 5 sets × 4 reps @ 80% 1RM.
- Weighted Pull-Up — 5 sets × 4 reps (add load accordingly).

Accessory work maintains the Week 4 loads and rep ranges. The increased intensity on primary lifts is sufficient stimulus — do not also increase accessory loads this week.

Introduce **rest-pause sets** on one accessory exercise per session. Choose one exercise per day — for example, the incline dumbbell press on Monday, the chest-supported row on Tuesday — and perform it as a rest-pause set: take the set to within one rep of failure, rack the weight, rest 15 seconds, perform as many additional reps as possible, rest 15 seconds, perform a final cluster. This technique extends a set beyond normal failure and is a powerful hypertrophy tool. Use it on one exercise only per session — it is demanding and should not be overused.

---

### Week 6 — Top Sets and Back-Off Sets

The primary lifts move to a **top set / back-off structure** this week. This is the most important structural change of the upper body phase and the one most likely to drive the biggest strength gains.

**How it works:** Perform one top set at RPE 9 — genuinely heavy, one rep left in the tank at most. Then reduce the load by 10–12% and perform two back-off sets at the original rep range. The top set trains the nervous system to handle near-maximal loads. The back-off sets accumulate volume at a weight that now feels manageable by comparison.

**Week 6 primary lift prescription:**

- Bench Press — 1 top set × 3 reps @ RPE 9, then 2 × 5 reps at 88% of top set load.
- Overhead Press — 1 top set × 3 reps @ RPE 9, then 2 × 5 reps at 88% of top set load.
- Pendlay Row — 1 top set × 3 reps @ RPE 9, then 2 × 5 reps at 88% of top set load.
- Weighted Pull-Up — 1 top set × 3 reps @ RPE 9, then 2 × 5 reps at reduced load.

Record the top set loads. These numbers are the new baseline for the return-to-full-programme phase.

---

### Week 7 — Volume Consolidation

Pull back slightly from the Week 6 intensity. Move to **4 sets × 5 reps** on all primary lifts at approximately 82–85% 1RM. This is not a deload — loads are still heavy — but the removal of the RPE 9 top set gives the nervous system a partial recovery while volume is maintained. Think of it as a consolidation week: the adaptations from Weeks 5 and 6 are being absorbed.

Increase accessory loads across the board where Week 6 felt below RPE 7. The accessories have been at relatively stable loads for several weeks and are ready for a push.

By the end of Week 7, the physio review should be occurring. If clearance is given to begin reintroducing posterior-chain work, Phase C of the injury management plan begins on the lower body add-on days. The upper body programme continues uninterrupted regardless of the physio outcome.

---

### Week 8 — True Deload

Four weeks of elevated upper body volume and two weeks of genuine intensification warrant a proper deload. Reduce all loads by 35–40%, cut to 3 sets per exercise, and reduce session length by 20 minutes. Keep the four-session structure — the frequency is maintained, the load is not. The client should leave every session this week feeling like she could have done significantly more. That feeling is the point.

Use this week for technique work. Film the bench press and overhead press from the side. Assess bar path, elbow position, and shoulder blade movement. Film the pull-up from the side and assess scapular depression and chin-over-bar position. Technique refinements made during a deload, when the client is not fatigued, tend to stick better than corrections made mid-heavy-set.

---

## Conditioning Sessions — Upper Body and Cardio Only

The conditioning sessions are fully revised to remove any lower body demand beyond easy cycling. The hamstring is not loaded, stretched, or fatigued in any conditioning session during the restricted phase.

**Wednesday — Steady State Cardio**

Stationary bike only. 30 minutes at RPE 4–5. The bike is the one cardio modality that can be performed comfortably with a healing hamstring — the seated position and circular pedalling motion involve minimal hamstring stretch or loading. Avoid the rower, ski erg, and treadmill entirely until clearance is given.

**Saturday — Upper Body Conditioning Circuit**

This session replaces the posterior-chain-focused circuit from the original plan with a format that elevates heart rate and builds upper body work capacity simultaneously. It is genuinely hard and genuinely productive — not a consolation session.

*Weeks 3–5 Saturday Circuit (4 rounds, 90 seconds rest between rounds):*

- Battle Rope Slam — 20 reps
- Push-Up (weighted vest if available) — 15 reps
- TRX or Ring Row — 15 reps
- Dumbbell Push Press — 12 reps
- Seated Cable Row — 15 reps
- Plate Ground-to-Overhead — 10 reps
- Rest 90 seconds, repeat

The plate ground-to-overhead deserves a note: the client picks a plate up from the floor and presses it overhead. This involves a slight hip hinge to pick up the plate — monitor carefully in the first session. If any hamstring discomfort is felt, replace it with a dumbbell thruster performed from a standing position.

*Weeks 6–7 Saturday EMOM (24 minutes):*

- Minute A: 15 Battle Rope Slams + 8 Push-Ups
- Minute B: 12 Dumbbell Push Press
- Minute C: 15 TRX Rows + 10 Face Pulls

Repeat A–B–C sequence 8 times. The rest within each minute rewards efficient work. If the client is consistently getting less than 15 seconds of rest, reduce reps by 2 per exercise.

*Week 8 Deload Saturday:* Easy bike 20 minutes, then 2 rounds of the circuit at 60% effort.

## Nutrition During the Injury Phase

With lower body training significantly reduced, total energy expenditure drops. This is worth addressing directly with the client — not to restrict food, but to ensure she is eating in a way that supports the upper body training she is doing and the tissue healing that is happening simultaneously.

**Protein remains the priority.** Tissue repair demands amino acids. If anything, the protein target of 1.6–2.0 g per kg of bodyweight becomes more important during injury recovery, not less. Ensure the client is hitting this consistently.

**Total calories can reduce modestly** — perhaps 150–200 kcal below the previous target — to reflect the reduced lower body training volume. This is not aggressive restriction. It simply acknowledges that she is doing less total work and does not need the same fuel. If the client is already lean or has any history of disordered eating, skip this adjustment entirely and maintain previous intake.

**Anti-inflammatory foods** are worth emphasising during the acute healing phase — oily fish, berries, leafy greens, turmeric, and adequate omega-3 intake. These are not magic, but they support the inflammatory process that drives tissue repair and there is no downside to prioritising them.

**Sleep** becomes even more important during injury recovery. Tissue repair happens primarily during sleep. If the client is sleeping less than seven hours, this is the single highest-leverage intervention available to her right now — more impactful than any supplement or dietary adjustment.

---

## Tracking and Motivation

Give the client two tracking tools that make progress visible during this phase.

**First**, a simple weekly log of the top set load on bench press, overhead press, Pendlay row, and weighted pull-up. Watching these numbers climb week over week is concrete evidence that the programme is working despite the injury.

**Second**, a pull-up progression tracker. Whether she is working toward her first bodyweight pull-up or adding load to existing pull-ups, this is a goal with a clear endpoint that can be achieved within the injury timeframe. Pull-ups are also highly visible — there is something uniquely satisfying about being able to do something you could not do before, and that satisfaction matters when a client is frustrated.

Frame every session around what she *can* do, not what she cannot. She is building a stronger upper body, a more resilient posterior chain through careful rehabilitation, and a more complete understanding of her own training. When she returns to the deadlift, she will be pulling with a stronger back, better lat engagement, and more upper body structural integrity than she had before the injury. The hamstring strain, managed correctly, may ultimately make her a better deadlifter.

# Weeks 7–12 Revised
### Physio Clearance: Moderate Hip-Hinge, RPE 6 Max, 3-Week Build, No Heavy Deadlifts Yet

---

## What This Changes and Why

This is genuinely good news and worth framing that way with the client. The physio has cleared hip-hinge movement under load ahead of the six-week outer boundary, which means the tissue is healing well. The restriction is specific and sensible — RPE 6 maximum means the hamstring is being loaded but not stressed, and the three-week build gives a clear progressive structure to work within.

The upper body intensification continues without interruption. The posterior-chain reintroduction runs alongside it as a parallel track, building from cautious to confident over Weeks 7 through 9, before the full programme structure reasserts itself in Weeks 10 through 12.

Three rules govern every posterior-chain decision from here:

**Rule one — RPE 6 is a ceiling, not a target.** If a set feels like it is approaching RPE 6, the load is reduced or the set ends. There is no benefit to testing the boundary.

**Rule two — Pain is an immediate stop signal.** Discomfort, tightness, or any sensation in the right hamstring that was not present at the start of the set means the exercise stops, the load comes down, and the trainer notes exactly what movement and load triggered it.

**Rule three — The deadlift earns its way back.** The conventional deadlift does not return until the Romanian deadlift, hip thrust, and back extension have all been trained for at least two weeks at RPE 6 without any hamstring response. It returns at the lightest possible load and builds from there.

| **Week 7** | Hinge reintroduction — bodyweight and very light load, RPE 4–5 | Continued intensification |
| **Week 8** | Light loaded hinges — RPE 5–6, range of motion building | Top set / back-off structure |
| **Week 9** | Moderate loaded hinges — RPE 6, full ROM if pain-free | Volume consolidation |
| **Week 10** | Conventional deadlift returns — light, RPE 6 max | Upper body deload then rebuild |

## WEEK 7 — Hinge Reintroduction

### Lower Body

The first week back into hinge movements is about **pattern rehearsal and tissue assessment**, not loading. The hamstring needs to experience the movement under minimal load and report back. Every set this week is diagnostic as much as it is training.

**Monday Lower Body Add-On (20 minutes, after Push A session):**

Warm-up addition: Before the lower body work, spend 5 minutes on the stationary bike and perform **neural flossing** — confirm the specific technique with the physio, but the general principle involves gentle sciatic nerve mobilisation through repeated ankle dorsiflexion and plantarflexion with the leg extended. This primes the tissue without loading it.

- Bodyweight Romanian Deadlift — 3 sets × 10 reps. No load whatsoever. The goal is to feel the hamstring move through the hinge pattern and identify any restriction, tightness, or discomfort. Hinge until a mild stretch is felt — do not push into the end range. If this is pain-free, proceed to the next exercise. If any discomfort is felt, stop here and inform the physio.
- Glute Bridge (bodyweight, bilateral) — 3 sets × 15 reps. One-second pause at the top. This loads the glute and hamstring in a shortened position — the least provocative form of posterior-chain loading available.
- Leg Press — 3 sets × 12 reps (maintained from previous weeks).
- Leg Extension — 3 sets × 12 reps.
- Terminal Knee Extension — 2 sets × 15 reps each leg.

**Thursday Lower Body Add-On (20 minutes, after Push B session):**

If Monday was fully pain-free:

- Romanian Deadlift (empty bar — 20 kg) — 3 sets × 8 reps. The first loaded hinge since the injury. Twenty kilograms is the load regardless of what the client was lifting before. Lower the bar to just below the knee — do not chase the floor yet. Three-second eccentric. Full attention on hamstring sensation throughout.
- Hip Thrust (bodyweight only) — 3 sets × 12 reps. Progress from the glute bridge by adding the bench elevation, which increases the range of hip extension.
- Leg Press — 3 sets × 10 reps.
- Leg Extension — 3 sets × 12 reps.
- Terminal Knee Extension — 2 sets × 15 reps each leg.

If Thursday's empty bar Romanian deadlift produces any hamstring response, return to bodyweight only and hold there for another week before attempting load again.

### Upper Body

The upper body programme continues exactly as prescribed in the Week 7 plan from the previous document — **4 sets × 5 reps on all primary lifts at 82–85% 1RM**, accessory loads increasing across the board. The posterior-chain reintroduction is a separate track and does not reduce upper body training in any way.

---

## WEEK 8 — Light Loaded Hinges, RPE 5–6

### Lower Body

Assuming Week 7 was fully pain-free, Week 8 introduces modest loading on the hinge movements. The loads named below are starting points — adjust based on the client's response and the RPE ceiling. If a suggested load feels above RPE 6, reduce it. The RPE ceiling is more important than any specific kilogram figure.

**Monday Lower Body Add-On:**

- Romanian Deadlift — 3 sets × 8 reps @ 30–40 kg. Three-second eccentric. Range of motion extends slightly further than Week 7 — aim for mid-shin rather than just below the knee, provided no hamstring tension is felt. RPE should be 4–5 at most. This should feel almost embarrassingly light. That is correct.
- Hip Thrust (barbell, 20 kg added) — 3 sets × 12 reps. The first loaded hip thrust. Full hip extension at the top, one-second pause.
- Back Extension (bodyweight) — 3 sets × 12 reps. Controlled movement, glute and hamstring initiation, no hyperextension at the top.
- Leg Press — 3 sets × 10 reps.
- Leg Extension — 3 sets × 12 reps.

**Thursday Lower Body Add-On:**

If Monday was pain-free, add a small load increase and extend range of motion slightly:

- Romanian Deadlift — 3 sets × 8 reps @ 35–45 kg. Range of motion now approaching the floor if comfortable. Three-second eccentric maintained. RPE 5–6.
- Hip Thrust — 3 sets × 10 reps (same load as Monday or very slightly heavier).
- Back Extension — 3 sets × 12 reps (bodyweight, same as Monday).
- Hack Squat — 3 sets × 10 reps.
- Leg Extension — 3 sets × 12 reps.
- Terminal Knee Extension — 2 sets × 15 reps each leg.

One important note on the Romanian deadlift range of motion: **full range means the bar reaches the floor with a neutral spine and a strong hamstring stretch felt bilaterally**. Do not push to full range until it arrives naturally and pain-free. Some clients will reach full range in Week 8. Others will need another week. Follow the tissue, not the calendar.

### Upper Body

Week 8 is the **upper body deload** as previously planned. Reduce all loads by 35–40%, cut to 3 sets per exercise, reduce session length. The four-session structure is maintained. Use the reduced intensity to film technique on the bench press and pull-up and address any form issues identified during the intensification weeks.

The deload timing works well here — the upper body backs off slightly just as the lower body is beginning to demand more attention and mental focus. The client is not trying to push hard in two directions simultaneously.

## WEEK 9 — Moderate Loaded Hinges, RPE 6

### Lower Body

This is the final week of the physio-prescribed three-week build. By the end of this week, the client should be performing Romanian deadlifts and hip thrusts at a load that genuinely challenges her within the RPE 6 ceiling. The back extension can begin to add a small amount of load. The conventional deadlift is still absent — it returns in Week 10 only if Week 9 is fully pain-free.

**Monday Lower Body — Now a Standalone Session**

From Week 9, the lower body work is substantial enough to warrant its own session rather than being bolted onto the end of a push session. Restructure Monday as follows: the push session moves to the morning or is separated by at least four hours from the lower body session. If same-session training is the only option, perform lower body first — it is the higher priority at this stage of the rehabilitation.

- Romanian Deadlift — 4 sets × 8 reps. Load should be at RPE 6 on the final set — approximately 50–60% of the pre-injury working load, though this varies by individual. Three-second eccentric. Full range of motion if Week 8 achieved it pain-free.
- Hip Thrust (barbell) — 4 sets × 10 reps. Load increases from Week 8. RPE 5–6.
- Back Extension — 3 sets × 12 reps. Add a light plate held at chest if bodyweight felt below RPE 5 in Week 8.
- Good Morning (empty bar) — 2 sets × 10 reps. The good morning is reintroduced at the lightest possible load. It trains the spinal erectors and hamstrings in the same position as the deadlift and is one of the most valuable accessories for rebuilding posterior-chain strength. Empty bar only this week — the movement pattern is the goal, not the load.
- Leg Press — 3 sets × 10 reps.
- Leg Extension — 3 sets × 12 reps.
- Dead Bug — 3 × 8 reps each side. Core stability work returns to the lower body session in preparation for loaded deadlifting next week.

**Thursday Lower Body — Standalone Session:**

- Romanian Deadlift — 4 sets × 6 reps. Slightly heavier than Monday if Monday was pain-free. RPE 6 ceiling strictly observed.
- Hip Thrust — 4 sets × 8 reps (heavier than Monday).
- Back Extension — 3 sets × 12 reps (same load as Monday or slightly heavier).
- Good Morning — 3 sets × 10 reps (empty bar, same as Monday — do not add load yet).
- Hack Squat — 3 sets × 10 reps.
- Leg Extension — 3 sets × 12 reps.
- Ab Wheel Rollout — 3 × 6 reps. Anti-extension core strength in preparation for deadlift loading.

### Upper Body

Upper body rebuilds from the Week 8 deload. Return to working loads — the same loads used in Week 7 — and re-establish the four-session structure at full intensity. The top set / back-off structure from Week 6 is reintroduced on the bench press and Pendlay row. RPE target on top sets is 8–9.

**Primary lift prescription for Week 9:**

- Bench Press — 1 top set × 3 reps @ RPE 8–9, then 2 × 5 at 88% of top set load.
- Overhead Press — 4 sets × 4 reps @ 80% 1RM.
- Pendlay Row — 1 top set × 3 reps @ RPE 8–9, then 2 × 5 at 88% of top set load.
- Weighted Pull-Up — 4 sets × 4 reps, heavier than Week 7.

## WEEK 10 — Conventional Deadlift Returns

### The Conversation Before the Session

Before Week 10's first lower body session, have an explicit conversation with the client about expectations. The deadlift is returning at a load that will feel insultingly light. That is intentional and correct. The goal of Week 10 is not to demonstrate strength — it is to reintroduce the movement pattern under load, assess the hamstring's response, and establish a new baseline from which to build. One session of ego-driven loading at this stage risks re-injury and another six weeks of rehabilitation. The light load is the smart load.

A practical starting point is **50% of her pre-injury working load** — not 50% of her 1RM, but 50% of what she was actually lifting in her working sets before the strain. If she was pulling 4 × 6 at 80 kg, she begins at 40 kg. This will feel easy. It should.

### Monday Lower Body

Warm-up: Stationary bike 8 minutes, neural flossing, banded clamshells 2 × 15, bodyweight Romanian deadlift 2 × 8, empty bar Romanian deadlift 1 × 5.

- Conventional Deadlift — 3 sets × 5 reps @ 50% pre-injury working load. Rest 3 full minutes between sets. Film every set from the side. Assess setup, bar path, and hamstring sensation. RPE should be 4–5 — if it feels heavier than that, reduce the load further. There is no floor on how light this can be.
- Romanian Deadlift — 3 sets × 8 reps (same load as Week 9 Thursday or very slightly heavier).
- Hip Thrust — 3 sets × 10 reps (progressing from Week 9).
- Back Extension — 3 sets × 10 reps (light plate).
- Good Morning — 3 sets × 10 reps (empty bar maintained — do not add load the same week the conventional deadlift returns).
- Dead Bug — 3 × 8 reps each side.

**If any hamstring discomfort occurs during the conventional deadlift:** Stop the deadlift immediately. Complete the remaining exercises. Do not attempt the deadlift again until the physio has been consulted. This is not a setback — it is information.

### Thursday Lower Body

If Monday was pain-free:

- Conventional Deadlift — 3 sets × 5 reps. Add 5 kg compared to Monday if Monday felt below RPE 5. If Monday felt like RPE 5, hold the same load. Do not add load if there was any hamstring sensation on Monday, even if it did not qualify as pain.
- Romanian Deadlift — 4 sets × 8 reps (progressing load).
- Hip Thrust — 4 sets × 10 reps (progressing load).
- Back Extension — 3 sets × 12 reps.
- Good Morning — 3 sets × 10 reps (add 5 kg if empty bar felt below RPE 4).
- Hack Squat — 3 sets × 8 reps.
- Ab Wheel Rollout — 3 × 8 reps.

### Upper Body

Upper body continues the Week 9 structure with load increases of 2.5–5 kg on primary lifts where Week 9 top sets felt below RPE 9. The upper body is now in a genuine strength phase — the bench press and row top set loads from Week 9 are the new floor, not the ceiling.

### Lower Body

Assuming two pain-free deadlift sessions in Week 10, the load increases meaningfully this week. The RPE ceiling rises from 6 to 7 — the physio's three-week build is complete and the tissue has demonstrated it can tolerate progressive loading. This is still not heavy deadlifting. RPE 7 means two to three reps clearly left in the tank. But it is a genuine training stimulus and the client will feel the difference.

**Monday Lower Body:**

- Conventional Deadlift — 4 sets × 4 reps. Load at RPE 6–7 on working sets — approximately 60–65% of pre-injury 1RM. Rest 3–4 minutes between sets.
- Romanian Deadlift — 4 sets × 8 reps @ RPE 6–7. Three-second eccentric. Full range of motion.
- Hip Thrust — 4 sets × 8 reps (heavier than Week 10).
- Back Extension — 3 sets × 12 reps (plate at chest, progressing load).
- Good Morning — 3 sets × 8 reps (now with modest load — 30–40 kg, RPE 5–6).
- Nordic Hamstring Curl — 2 sets × 3 reps. The Nordic hamstring curl returns very cautiously. Eccentric only — lower as slowly as possible, use hands to return to the top. Two sets of three reps is sufficient for the first week back. This exercise is one of the most effective hamstring strengthening and injury-prevention tools available, and reintroducing it now builds resilience for the heavier loading ahead.
- Dead Bug — 3 × 8 reps each side.

**Thursday Lower Body:**

- Conventional Deadlift — 4 sets × 4 reps. Add 5 kg compared to Monday if Monday was pain-free and felt below RPE 7.
- Romanian Deadlift — 4 sets × 6 reps (heavier than Monday, RPE 7).
- Hip Thrust — 4 sets × 8 reps (same or slightly heavier than Monday).
- Back Extension — 3 sets × 12 reps.
- Good Morning — 3 sets × 8 reps (same load as Monday).
- Nordic Hamstring Curl — 2 sets × 4 reps.
- Ab Wheel Rollout — 3 × 8 reps.

### Upper Body

Upper body moves to a **strength maintenance** structure this week. The heavy intensification work of Weeks 9 and 10 has done its job. With the lower body now demanding more attention and the programme approaching its final week, the upper body shifts to preserving the strength gains made rather than pushing for new ones.

**Primary lift prescription for Week 11:**

- Bench Press — 3 sets × 3 reps @ 85% 1RM. Heavy but not maximal. The nervous system is primed without being taxed.
- Overhead Press — 3 sets × 4 reps @ 80% 1RM.
- Pendlay Row — 3 sets × 3 reps @ 85% 1RM.
- Weighted Pull-Up — 3 sets × 3 reps (heavy).

Accessory work reduces to two sets per exercise at moderate loads. Sessions are shorter this week — the client should leave feeling sharp and powerful, not depleted.
